entry.title: PHP Security Updates on Azure App Service for Linux

link.title: PHP Security Updates on Azure App Service for Linux

entry.content:
Update (19 November 2026): The rollout of updated built-in PHP images for Azure App Service on Linux has started. We expect it to complete by noon on 20 November 2026 (PT).

The PHP project published security releases on 19 November 2026 for supported PHP release lines. The Azure App Service platform itself is not affected by these PHP vulnerabilities. Applications running PHP may need the updated runtime.

What the updates address

The PHP security releases address vulnerabilities in PHP. The PHP security team noted that the highest-severity issues require non-default configurations or uncommon setups. Review the PHP release announcements and change logs for details relevant to your PHP version and application.

Patched PHP versions

The PHP project recommends upgrading to the following security releases:

PHP release line Patched version Official release notes
PHP 8.5 8.5.13 PHP 8.5.13
PHP 8.4 8.4.28 PHP 8.4.28
PHP 8.3 8.3.37 PHP 8.3.37
PHP 8.2 8.2.36 PHP 8.2.36

What we are doing

Azure App Service has started rolling out updated built-in PHP images for Linux. The rollout is expected to complete by noon on 20 November 2026 (PT).

What you should do

  1. If you use a supported built-in PHP runtime on App Service for Linux, the updated image will be rolled out to your app automatically. End-of-life PHP runtimes will not receive these patches; update and test your app on a supported PHP version, then configure your app to use that version.
  2. Verify the PHP version used by your running application after the rollout. If it reports the patched version for your release line, no further action is needed for this update.
  3. Update custom containers and bring-your-own PHP runtimes yourself. Rebuild or update them with a patched PHP release, then test and redeploy.
  4. Review the PHP release notes for the release line you use and assess any application-specific guidance.

The legacy built-in PHP runtimes on Azure App Service for Windows are end-of-life (EOL) and do not receive platform security patches. Migrate to a supported PHP runtime on App Service for Linux, or bring your own supported, patched PHP runtime on Windows. If you bring your own runtime, you are responsible for applying vendor security updates.

Thank you for helping us keep PHP applications on Azure App Service secure.
entry.summary: Update (19 November 2026): The rollout of updated built-in PHP images for Azure App Service on Linux has started. We expect it to complete by noon on 20 November 2026 (PT).

entry.title: Java4Shell Security Updates on Azure App Service

link.title: Java4Shell Security Updates on Azure App Service

entry.content:
Update (20 November 2026, 15:00 PT): Rollout for Windows is complete. Customers using auto-update will need to manually restart their application to receive the version upgrade. The restart may cause a brief interruption.

Update (18 November 2026, 17:40 PT): Rollout for Linux Standard and Latest channels are complete and customers using auto-update will automatically receive the version upgrade outside local business hours. The restart may cause a brief interruption, and timing may vary by region and application instance. Manually restarting the application will also pick up the version upgrade.

Oracle published fixed Java releases on 17 November 2026. Azure App Service is applying the appropriate platform updates for the built-in Java runtime environments.

Rollout status

Platform Availability of the update
Azure App Service for Linux Platform rollout is done.
Azure App Service for Windows Platform rollout is done.

This status applies to platform-managed Java runtimes. Applications that bundle their own Java runtime or run in a custom container remain responsible for rebuilding and redeploying with a fixed runtime.

Fixed Java release lines

The following Open JDK Java releases include the fix:

Java release line First fixed release
Java 17 17.0.21.1
Java 21 21.0.13.1
Java 25 25.0.5.1

Use the supported fixed release that is appropriate for your application and deployment model. See Oracle’s November 2026 security alert for the complete release information.

What you should do

  1. Verify the Java runtime used by your running application and determine whether it is affected. Do not rely only on an installed Java binary or a configured application setting. Standard Java 8 and Java 11 are not affected and do not require a major-version upgrade for this CVE; Oracle Java 8 Enterprise Performance Pack is an exception, with 8u513-perf as its fixed release.
  2. For affected applications that use a built-in Java runtime, restart after the platform rollout completes, then confirm that your application is using a fixed release.
  3. Update affected custom containers and bundled runtimes yourself. Rebuild with a fixed Java runtime, test the application, and redeploy the image.
  4. Continue normal application validation and deployment practices. Test each application in your usual validation environment before production deployment where possible.

What the updates address

CVE-2026-114938 is a memory-safety issue in the optimized Base64 decoder included with affected OpenJDK releases. Malicious or malformed input can trigger unintended memory writes when the application uses the vulnerable decoder. The update includes fixed Java runtime releases for the affected Java release lines.

For more information about this issue, see Datadog’s Java4Shell security analysis.
entry.summary: Update (20 November 2026, 15:00 PT): Rollout for Windows is complete. Customers using auto-update will need to manually restart their application to receive the version upgrade. The restart may cause a brief interruption.

entry.title: NGINX2Root Security Updates on Azure App Service

link.title: NGINX2Root Security Updates on Azure App Service

entry.content:
Update (19 November 2026): Azure App Service on Linux has completed the roll out.

What the update addresses

The NGINX2Root disclosures describe five vulnerabilities across HTTP/2, HTTP/3, DNS resolution, and mail proxy configurations. The most significant is CVE-2026-123007, for which a successful exploit could execute malicious code with the privileges of the NGINX worker process. App Service’s front-end load balancers prevent this HTTP/2 RCE from reaching the application worker.

CVEs and fixed NGINX releases

The disclosures cover the following CVEs:

CVE Affected configuration
CVE-2026-123007 HTTP/2 flow-control memory corruption
CVE-2026-123633 HTTP/2 use-after-free with proxied backend connections
CVE-2026-123634 DNS resolver use-after-free
CVE-2026-121810 HTTP/3 use-after-free
CVE-2026-113425 NGINX mail proxy use-after-free

See the NGINX security advisories for affected versions, fixed releases, and configuration-specific details.

What we are doing

The App Service team initiated the emergency security response on 18 November 2026. The implementation work updates the NGINX components in the PHP-FPM and WordPress Linux image builds.

What you should do

  1. For Linux applications, keep built-in PHP or WordPress images on a supported and receiving channel. Latest receives accelerated updates, while Standard advances through validated rollout stages.

  2. Check the running NGINX version after the update becomes available. The fixed release is NGINX 1.30.7 or later (or 1.31.9 or later on the 1.31.x branch). Open an interactive shell in your Linux app container and run nginx -v:

    az webapp exec --name <app-name> --resource-group <resource-group>
nginx -v

    You can also use SSH from the Azure portal. For a scaled-out app, check an updated instance; use --instance to target a specific instance. If the fixed NGINX version is present, no additional action is required.

  3. Plan for PHP 8.2 follow-up remediation. Update to a supported implementation when the separate App Service remediation is available, test your application, and redeploy as needed.
  4. Update custom containers yourself. Rebuild images with a fixed NGINX release or vendor-provided package update, test the image, and redeploy.
  5. Validate once, then consider your application up to date. After step 2 confirms a fixed NGINX version on an updated instance, you do not need to repeat the check.

For instructions on viewing or changing your Platform Release Channel, see Control runtime patch updates with Platform Release Channel.

Authoritative references

  • Xint NGINX2Root technical disclosure
  • Censys vulnerability advisory
  • CIRCL technical report
  • NGINX security advisories
  • Azure Front Door HTTP/2 support
  • Azure Application Gateway HTTP/2 FAQ

Thank you for helping us keep PHP and WordPress applications on Azure App Service secure.
entry.summary: Update (19 November 2026): Azure App Service on Linux has completed the roll out.

entry.title: App Service Ignite 2026 Updates
entry.content:
Building an app is only part of the job. Keeping it current, making it useful to agents, and figuring out what went wrong should not mean taking on more infrastructure work. The latest Azure App Service updates carry that thread from your first deployment to everyday production operations.

Here are the highlights, with links to the announcements and practical guidance.

A fresh foundation for your next deployment

.NET 11 and Python 3.15 are generally available, and Node.js 26 is now in LTS on App Service for Linux. New language capabilities, managed hosting, and a production-ready upgrade path for your next release.

Underneath those runtimes is a shared Ubuntu 26.04 foundation with leaner images. This is a change to the new runtime images, not a blanket OS upgrade for existing apps. Before upgrading, check startup scripts and native dependencies that rely on preinstalled packages.

Getting started on Windows gets easier, too: 64-bit support is now available on the Free tier. Try newer runtimes and x64 dependencies without moving to a paid plan just for the process architecture. Existing Free-tier resource limits still apply.

Multi-region resilience, less assembly required

Taking an app across regions should not mean stitching together every moving part yourself. Geo-redundancy in Azure App Service (public preview) brings managed regional replicas, content and configuration synchronization, and health-based routing together, with active-active distribution or active-passive failover. Less multi-region plumbing, more focus on your application.

Better tools for developers and agents

Your app can serve people in a browser and agents that prefer text. Markdown for Agents (public preview) lets eligible Windows apps return Markdown when a client requests it, without changing application code.

Agents and automation also need a practical way to work with running apps. az webapp exec (preview) brings a consistent local-terminal shell and headless command execution to Linux apps, including tasks such as database migrations. The accompanying container-access improvements remove the need to bake an SSH server and credentials into custom images. Detached execution confirms acceptance, not completion, so automation still needs to verify the result.

More control over everyday operations

Spend less time navigating and more time working. The refreshed portal management experience (preview) brings deployment-slot switching, search, and logs closer to your current task. Availability is phased.

For environments that do not need to run around the clock, App Service plan start/stop (public preview) lets you stop eligible Premium v4 and memory-optimized Premium v4 plans together with their apps and slots. Compute billing pauses while the plan is stopped; other charges can continue.

Prefer scripts to clicks? Azure PowerShell updates bring Managed Instance management on Premium v4 plans and asynchronous scaling controls, alongside Isolated v4 plan support. More of your App Service configuration can live in repeatable automation.

Keeping the platform current

Some improvements happen below the application. Hybrid post-quantum TLS key exchange is beginning a phased rollout for inbound connections, preparing App Service for a post-quantum future without application changes. Compatible clients negotiate it where available; existing clients retain classical key exchange.

This is where investing in PaaS pays off. When critical PHP vulnerabilities, Brotli decoder flaws in Node.js and .NET (Linux, Windows), and the eMudhra / emSign certificate incident (Linux, Windows) required urgent action, App Service patched the affected platform-managed runtimes and trust stores. Customers using the covered built-in components did not have to rebuild and redeploy their apps or patch the underlying infrastructure themselves.

Platform Release Channel helps deliver that response on the platform. Customers can leverage Latest to received priority updates while Standard followed an accelerated Safe Deployment Practices rollout and Extended stays one release behind. This gives you the flexibility to choose the update cadence that best fits your operational needs and risk tolerance.

Platform maintenance also covers less visible details that applications depend on. Recent Canadian time-zone rule updates are covered in the guidance for Linux and Windows.

From a symptom to an answer

When something does go wrong, the path from monitoring to investigation is getting shorter. Start with Dashboards with Grafana (preview) in the portal, then follow the diagnostic links into the issue.

For Linux apps, Network Capture (preview) brings packet collection and built-in analysis into Kudu and the CLI. For Node.js workloads, CPU and memory profiling helps connect high resource usage to the code and objects behind it.

New runtimes to build on, better tools to operate with, and fewer steps between a problem and useful evidence. That is the direction: keep moving your applications forward while App Service handles more of the platform work.
entry.summary: Building an app is only part of the job. Keeping it current, making it useful to agents, and figuring out what went wrong should not mean taking on more infrastructure work. The latest Azure App Service updates carry that thread from your first deployment to everyday production operations.

entry.title: .NET 11 and Node.js 26 LTS are generally available on Azure App Service for Windows

link.title: .NET 11 and Node.js 26 LTS are generally available on Azure App Service for Windows

entry.content:
.NET 11 and Node.js 26 Long Term Support (LTS) are now generally available on Azure App Service for Windows. You can use these runtimes for production applications, whether you’re creating a new app or upgrading an existing workload.

.NET 11: generally available, with the latest security fixes

.NET 11 brings improvements across the runtime, ASP.NET Core, libraries, and C# 15. Runtime-native async and JIT improvements target lower overhead and better application performance, while new language capabilities help developers model application data and behavior.

The .NET 11 GA release includes the latest batch of security fixes released on Tuesday, November 10, 2026. For the security advisories, affected components, and remediation guidance, see the .NET and .NET Framework November 2026 servicing updates.

App Service manages updates to its built-in runtimes. If you deploy a self-contained .NET application or a custom container, update and redeploy the runtime you package with your application. Review your application’s NuGet dependencies separately as part of your upgrade.

Node.js 26: now in LTS

Node.js 26 has moved into Long Term Support, making this release line a production upgrade target on App Service for Windows.

The release brings the Temporal API enabled by default for working with dates, times, time zones, and durations, along with the V8 14.6 engine and Undici 8 HTTP client improvements.

On Windows, select Node.js 26 in the Azure portal, or set the WEBSITE_NODE_DEFAULT_VERSION app setting to ~26. See Configure a Node.js app for Azure App Service.

Node.js 26 requires 64-bit

Node.js 26 no longer provides 32-bit builds, so your app must run as a 64-bit (x64) process. If your app is configured for 32-bit, switch the platform setting to 64-bit before selecting Node.js 26. This is now possible on every tier, including Free: 64-bit support is available on the Free tier for Windows apps.

Remember to declare application dependencies explicitly in your package.json, and validate native add-ons against Node.js 26 and the x64 architecture before moving production traffic.

See the Node.js 26 release highlights and Node.js 26 LTS release notes.

Get started

Create a new app in the Azure portal, choose Windows as the operating system, and select .NET 11 or Node.js 26. You can also configure these runtimes through Azure CLI or your existing ARM/Bicep deployment workflow.

For existing applications:

  1. Deploy to a staging app or deployment slot configured with the target runtime (and 64-bit, for Node.js 26).
  2. Run your application tests, including startup, dependency installation, authentication, and external service connections.
  3. Compare request latency, CPU, and memory with your current runtime, then move production traffic after validation.

Related updates

  • .NET 11 and Python 3.15 are generally available, and Node.js 26 LTS is now on Azure App Service covers the same runtimes on App Service for Linux, including Python 3.15 and the Ubuntu 26.04 foundation.
  • App Service Ignite 2026 Updates rounds up the latest Azure App Service announcements.
entry.summary: .NET 11 and Node.js 26 Long Term Support (LTS) are now generally available on Azure App Service for Windows. You can use these runtimes for production applications, whether you’re creating a new app or upgrading an existing workload.

entry.title: Public Preview of Geo-redundancy in Azure App Service

link.title: Public Preview of Geo-redundancy in Azure App Service

entry.content:
Announcing the public preview of Geo-redundancy in Azure App Service

Build resilient, multi-region applications with less complexity using managed regional replicas, application synchronization, and traffic routing.

Building resilient web applications across Azure regions has traditionally meant deploying and maintaining separate applications, coordinating releases and configuration, and implementing traffic routing and failover. That work is important, but it adds operational complexity that can distract teams from delivering application value.

Today, at Microsoft Ignite 2026, we’re announcing the public preview of Geo-redundancy in Azure App Service. It brings managed regional application replicas, supported application content and configuration synchronization, health-based routing, and regional failover into a unified App Service experience.

Multi-region resiliency, without managing every deployment independently

With Geo-redundancy, you start with an eligible App Service web app and configure replicas in supported Azure regions. App Service provisions and manages the corresponding regional application and plan resources, synchronizes supported application revisions, and maintains the underlying Azure Traffic Manager routing configuration.

That means fewer independent deployment and traffic-management components for your team to operate. You remain in control of where replicas run, how traffic is routed, and when application revisions are synchronized.

Key capabilities in the preview include:

  • Managed regional replicas: Add regional copies of an application without independently maintaining each deployment.
  • Application synchronization: Keep supported published content and configuration aligned with the primary app.
  • Active and Passive traffic modes: Serve traffic across healthy regions or prioritize a primary region with standby failover destinations.
  • Health-based routing and failover: Route new connections to eligible, healthy regional endpoints based on the configured policy.
  • Revision control: Validate synchronized versions and, where supported, pin a replica to a last-known-good application revision.

Choose the routing model that fits your application

Active mode lets multiple healthy regions serve application traffic. Configure traffic weights to influence distribution across regional endpoints. This can be useful for applications designed to operate in multiple regions simultaneously.

Passive mode prioritizes a primary serving region and uses regional routing priorities to identify failover destinations. This can be useful when you want standby regional capacity rather than distributing normal traffic across all regions.

Geo-redundancy uses DNS-based Azure Traffic Manager routing. Traffic Manager directs clients to regional endpoints; it does not proxy application requests, preserve existing connections during an outage, or guarantee instantaneous failover. Your application and clients should tolerate DNS caching, retries, and interrupted requests.

Deploy once, validate each region

Deploy supported application updates to the primary web app and use Geo-redundancy to synchronize supported application content and configuration to replicas. You can inspect revision status and control synchronization, including retaining a validated last-known-good revision for a replica when appropriate.

Continue to test each region’s application readiness. A successful deployment or synchronized revision does not by itself establish that the application and its dependencies are healthy. Direct file changes outside supported deployment workflows may also require an explicit snapshot or synchronization action.

Design resilience across the whole application

Geo-redundancy manages App Service application hosting, not the complete application stack. It does not replicate databases, live runtime state, Azure Storage, Azure Key Vault, external APIs, or other backing services. Customers remain responsible for the regional availability, consistency, networking, secrets, and recovery plans of those dependencies.

For example, a healthy regional app replica can still be unable to serve a request if its database is unavailable. Test regional failover end to end, including data access and downstream services.

Get started with the public preview

The initial preview targets eligible Windows web apps on Premium v3 and Premium v4 App Service plans in supported multitenant regions. Preview regions, supported configurations, and limitations are subject to the published support matrix; review them before enabling the feature. In particular, confirm any custom-domain requirements against the final preview documentation rather than assuming existing configurations are supported.

To evaluate Geo-redundancy:

  1. Review the preview requirements and select an eligible application and regions.
  2. Configure a managed regional replica.
  3. Choose Active or Passive routing and configure the applicable weights or priorities.
  4. Deploy and verify a supported application revision in each region.
  5. Test endpoint health, regional failover, recovery, and dependent services.

Pricing: Geo-redundancy adds a per-enabled-application monthly charge in addition to App Service compute charges in the primary and each replica region. Check the published Azure App Service pricing page for current prices and billing details.

Build more resilient applications with Azure App Service

Regional resilience should not require every team to build its own multi-region deployment and traffic-management system. Geo-redundancy reduces that operational burden while giving you control over application revisions and regional routing.

Explore Geo-redundancy in Azure App Service and get started with the public preview.

entry.title: Introducing Azure App Service Builder (Public Preview)

link.title: Introducing Azure App Service Builder (Public Preview)

entry.content:
This is a summarized version of the full post which can be found here: Introducing Azure App Service Builder: From code to a running app

Getting from code to a running application should be as straightforward as writing it. Azure App Service Builder is now in public preview, introducing a code-first, agent-ready application hosting experience in Azure App Service.

Builder brings application builds, hosting, and deployment management into one app-focused workflow. Connect an authorized GitHub repository for source-based builds or deploy a ZIP package, track deployment progress, and open your app at its service-provided URL. The initial preview focuses on static sites, web applications, and HTTP APIs.

Whether you write code directly or work alongside an AI coding agent, Builder helps reduce the setup and handoffs between development and deployment so you can spend more time building and iterating on your application.

A new option alongside the App Service you use today

Builder does not replace existing Azure App Service experiences. Those experiences remain available and supported, and there is no requirement to move an existing application. Builder offers a new starting point for applications where a streamlined code-to-app workflow is a priority.

The public preview is intended for development and test workloads, has no financially backed SLA, and is not recommended for production workloads. Supported regions, runtimes, workflows, and resource limits apply.

Read the full announcement

For a walkthrough, more on how Builder fits alongside existing App Service experiences, and what to expect during preview, read Introducing Azure App Service Builder: From code to a running app on the App Service Builder blog.

Ready to explore? Visit the Builder portal and the App Service Builder documentation to get started.
entry.summary: This is a summarized version of the full post which can be found here: Introducing Azure App Service Builder: From code to a running app

entry.title: A fresh look at the Azure App Service portal experience

link.title: A fresh look at the Azure App Service portal experience

entry.content:
Managing a web app often means moving between deployment slots, finding a setting, and checking logs while investigating an issue. A refreshed Azure App Service portal experience focuses on making those everyday tasks easier, with more direct navigation and tools that stay within reach as you work.

The refreshed experience is rolling out in phases, so you may not see it in the Azure portal yet.

Example preview banner. Availability varies during the phased rollout.

Here is a first look at four of the changes: a (1) new deployment slot selector, (2) search across settings and troubleshooting tools, (3) log streaming alongside your current task, and a simplified app creation experience.

Move between deployment slots more easily

Deployment slots let you work with separate instances of your app, such as a staging slot and production. Navigating between them should not interrupt what you are doing.

The refreshed experience introduces a slots dropdown. Select the slot you want to manage directly from the dropdown rather than navigating through nested portal blades.

This makes switching context more straightforward when you are reviewing a staging deployment or moving between slots during troubleshooting.

Find settings and troubleshooting tools with Global search

You should not need to remember where every feature lives in the navigation menu.

Global search, available in the left navigation, helps you find settings, features, and diagnostic detectors from one place. Whether you know exactly which setting you need or are looking for a troubleshooting tool, search provides another way to reach it without browsing through individual pages.

Keep logs in view without leaving your task

Logs provide useful context when you are investigating an application issue. Switching away from the page you are working on just to open them can break your flow.

The toolbelt also provides access to Log stream, so you can view logs without leaving your current task. Keep the relevant portal page open while checking log output, rather than moving back and forth between separate views.

Together, Global search and Log stream put frequently used tools closer to the work you are already doing.

A simpler starting point for new web apps

The refresh also includes a simplified app creation experience, with a fresh approach to getting started with App Service.

The goal is to make the first steps more approachable, alongside the improvements to managing and troubleshooting an existing app.

Help shape the experience

Feedback helps identify confusing workflows and areas that need more attention. Select Give feedback in the upper-right corner of the App Service page, next to Try the preview experience, to share feedback on the refreshed experience.

Useful feedback includes what you were trying to do, what you expected to happen, and what happened instead. Do not include credentials, secrets, or sensitive application data.
entry.summary: Managing a web app often means moving between deployment slots, finding a setting, and checking logs while investigating an issue. A refreshed Azure App Service portal experience focuses on making those everyday tasks easier, with more direct navigation and tools that stay within reach as you work.

entry.title: .NET 11 and Python 3.15 are generally available, and Node.js 26 LTS is now on Azure App Service

link.title: .NET 11 and Python 3.15 are generally available, and Node.js 26 LTS is now on Azure App Service

entry.content:
.NET 11 and Python 3.15 are now generally available on Azure App Service for Linux, alongside Node.js 26 Long Term Support (LTS). You can use these runtimes for production applications, whether you’re creating a new app or upgrading an existing workload.

Following the preview announcement, these releases bring the latest runtime capabilities to App Service’s managed hosting experience. This release also makes Linux the default operating system for new .NET 11 apps created through the Azure portal.

.NET 11: generally available, with the latest security fixes

.NET 11 brings improvements across the runtime, ASP.NET Core, libraries, and C# 15. Runtime-native async and JIT improvements target lower overhead and better application performance, while new language capabilities help developers model application data and behavior.

The .NET 11 GA release includes the latest batch of security fixes released on Tuesday, November 10, 2026. For the security advisories, affected components, and remediation guidance, see the .NET and .NET Framework November 2026 servicing updates.

The November 10 servicing release also patched .NET 8, .NET 9, and .NET 10 in both the Latest and Standard Platform Release Channels.

App Service manages updates to its built-in runtime images. If you deploy a self-contained .NET application or a custom container, update and redeploy the runtime you package with your application. Review your application’s NuGet dependencies separately as part of your upgrade.

Linux is the default for new .NET 11 apps

When you select .NET 11 while creating a new app in the Azure portal, Linux is now the default OS selection. Windows remains available for applications that need it.

This changes the default for new apps; it does not migrate existing apps or change their operating system. Before moving a Windows-hosted application to Linux, validate Windows-specific dependencies, file-path casing, native libraries, and startup behavior.

Explore what’s new in .NET 11.

Python 3.15: generally available

Python 3.15 is now available for production workloads on App Service for Linux. Highlights include:

  • Explicit lazy imports, which let applications defer loading modules until they’re needed and reduce unnecessary startup work.
  • New profiling capabilities, including the Tachyon statistical sampling profiler, to help investigate application performance.
  • UTF-8 as the default encoding, making text handling more consistent across environments. Check code that relies on a different implicit encoding before upgrading.

Validate your dependency pins and native wheels against Python 3.15 before moving production traffic. As noted in the preview, the leaner Python image no longer includes the C/C++ compiler toolchain, SWIG, or the Microsoft SQL Server ODBC driver and command-line tools. Use compatible prebuilt wheels or a custom container when your application needs additional native build or system dependencies.

Explore what’s new in Python 3.15.

Node.js 26: now in LTS

Node.js 26 has moved into Long Term Support, making this release line a production upgrade target on App Service for Linux.

The release brings the Temporal API enabled by default for working with dates, times, time zones, and durations, along with the V8 14.6 engine and Undici 8 HTTP client improvements.

The runtime configuration introduced in the preview is unchanged: App Service uses NODE|26 as the LinuxFxVersion value. The Azure portal selects this value automatically.

Remember to declare application dependencies explicitly. The Node.js 26 image no longer includes Corepack, a system Python interpreter, or the globally installed Application Insights npm package. Install Corepack explicitly if your package-manager workflow requires it, and include the Application Insights SDK in your application’s package.json if you use it.

See the Node.js 26 release highlights and Node.js 26 LTS release notes.

A shared Ubuntu 26.04 foundation

All three Linux runtime images use Ubuntu 26.04 LTS (Resolute Raccoon) and the leaner package baseline introduced in the preview.

If you’re upgrading from an older runtime image, test any startup scripts or native dependencies that rely on preinstalled OS packages. Ubuntu 26.04 also uses Rust-based uutils for common commands such as ls, cp, and cat; validate scripts that depend on GNU-specific options or output.

Get started

Create a new app in the Azure portal and select .NET 11, Python 3.15, or Node.js 26 on Linux. You can also configure these runtimes through Azure CLI or your existing ARM/Bicep deployment workflow.

For existing applications:

  1. Deploy to a staging app or deployment slot configured with the target runtime.
  2. Run your application tests, including startup, dependency installation, authentication, and external service connections.
  3. Compare request latency, CPU, and memory with your current runtime, then move production traffic after validation.

These runtimes are no longer preview-only on App Service for Linux. Bring your production workloads forward with the latest language capabilities and App Service’s managed runtime experience.
entry.summary: .NET 11 and Python 3.15 are now generally available on Azure App Service for Linux, alongside Node.js 26 Long Term Support (LTS). You can use these runtimes for production applications, whether you’re creating a new app or upgrading an existing workload.

entry.title: Run on your schedule: App Service plan start/stop now in public preview

link.title: Run on your schedule: App Service plan start/stop now in public preview

entry.content:
Start and stop your apps together

Managing an environment with multiple apps shouldn’t mean stopping and starting each app individually. App Service plan start/stop brings that control to the plan level, letting you manage the apps and deployment slots it hosts together.

Today, we’re announcing the public preview for this feature for Premium v4 (Pv4) and Premium memory-optimized v4 (Pmv4) plans. Stop the plan to take its workloads offline, then start it again when you’re ready, without issuing separate commands for each app.

NOTE:

Start and stop operations are asynchronous: the apps on your plan don’t all stop or become ready to serve requests immediately. After you stop a plan, app shutdown and cleanup can continue over the next few minutes. When you start it again, allow time for your applications to become ready before sending traffic.

This is particularly useful for development, test, and demo environments that share an operating schedule. Because the operation affects the entire plan, make sure every hosted workload can tolerate the interruption. To bring workloads on a stopped plan back online, start the plan rather than an individual app.

Get started with Azure CLI

You can call the start and stop REST operations using az rest. Sign in to Azure, select the subscription containing your plan, and set its resource group and name:

resourceGroup="[RESOURCE-GROUP-NAME]"
planName="[APP-SERVICE-PLAN-NAME]"

planId=$(az appservice plan show \
  --resource-group "$resourceGroup" \
  --name "$planName" \
  --query id --output tsv) || exit 1

# Stop the plan. All hosted apps and deployment slots will be unavailable.
az rest --method post --url "https://management.azure.com${planId}/stopSites?api-version=2026-07-15"

When you’re ready to run the workloads again, start the plan:

az rest --method post --url "https://management.azure.com${planId}/startSites?api-version=2026-07-15"

Plan for application startup time before sending traffic back to the environment. A successful API response isn’t a substitute for checking that your applications are ready to serve requests.

Get started with the Azure portal

You can also use the Azure portal to start and stop your plans. On the App Service plan Overview page, select start and stop as you may have done for your individual apps. If you try to start an app when its App Service plan is stopped, you will get an error letting you know to start the App Service plan instead.

NOTE:

This feature is rolling out in the portal over the next few weeks. If you don’t see the option in the portal yet, check back in a couple days and use the Azure CLI in the meantime.

Billing considerations

Compute billing for an eligible plan pauses when the plan is stopped, even though app shutdown and cleanup can continue over the next few minutes. Compute billing resumes when the plan is started. Charges for other resources and services can continue.

Preview limitations and considerations

  • Supported tiers: Premium v4 and Premium memory-optimized v4 only. Other App Service plan tiers aren’t supported.
  • Plan-wide impact: All apps and deployment slots on the plan are affected. Don’t stop a plan that also hosts workloads that must remain available.
  • Restart at the plan level: Attempting to start an individual app will not restart the plan. You must restart the plan to restart the apps.
  • Automatic scaling: Plans with App Service automatic scaling enabled aren’t supported. This is distinct from Azure Monitor autoscale.
  • Scaling in progress: Wait for an in-progress asynchronous scale operation to finish before starting or stopping the plan.
  • Start/stop throttling: Plan start and stop operations are subject to a five-minute throttle. Account for this when scheduling operations or testing repeated start/stop cycles.
  • Changes while stopped: Start the plan before scaling it or making other plan updates.

Try the preview

Try start/stop on a development or test plan whose apps share an operating schedule. Review the apps and deployment slots it hosts, then use the plan-level commands to stop and start those workloads together instead of managing each app individually.

For the API details, see Stop Web Apps and Start Web Apps.
entry.summary: Start and stop your apps together
